turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, nice to meet you too. Well, I came in because... I guess since I started helping out with the safety trainings at work, I just can't seem to stop focusing on how I look. 

When I'm up there pointing things out to the line, I keep noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look. It really bothers me. And then... well, they take pictures for the company newsletter, and when I look at them, I start thinking my face looks completely crooked. I've brought it up to a few people, but they tell me they don't see what I'm talking about at all. It's just hard for me to get past it, so I figured I should talk to someone.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent preoccupation with perceived flaws in their appearance (wrinkly, uneven hands and a crooked face) that others report not seeing.

turns.doctor_question: Because these worries about your hands and face bother you so much, do you find yourself repeatedly checking or examining them, like in mirrors, photos, or by comparing them to other people?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, I do. Especially before a training class, or... sometimes I do these workshops at the senior center. Before I go out there, I’ll usually go check the bathroom mirror a few times. I'll put extra lotion on my hands to try and smooth them out, and I'll turn my face different ways in the mirror just to see how it looks. 

Sometimes I even catch myself asking a coworker if I look all right before I start. Doing all that... well, it ends up making me run a little behind schedule sometimes, but I still get myself there and get the job done.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors regarding appearance, including repeatedly checking the mirror from multiple angles, applying extra lotion, and seeking reassurance from coworkers.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe there really is something wrong with how your hands or face look?
turns.patient_response:
Well... I mean, I see it. When I look in the mirror or at those newsletter pictures, my face definitely looks crooked to me. And my hands just look awful. 

But... since my coworkers and my family keep telling me they don't see what I'm talking about, I guess I'm just not sure anymore. It sure looks real to me, but I don't know why nobody else can see it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports perceiving their face as crooked and hands as awful, while noting that family and coworkers do not see these flaws, consistent with preoccupation with perceived appearance defects not observable to others.

turns.doctor_question: Because of these worries about how your hands or face look, have you ever avoided going to a training, workshop, or other social situation?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't completely avoided going to them. It hasn't stopped me from doing my job or my volunteer work. But... well, like I mentioned, I'm definitely slower getting ready for the trainings because I get stuck at the mirror. 

I will say, though, I've started ducking out of the way when they try to take photos for the newsletter now. And I guess I find myself hesitating a bit before going to social events... things I used to just go to and enjoy without really thinking about it. So I still go, but it just takes a little more effort to get myself out the door these days.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient reports getting stuck at the mirror while getting ready and ducking out of photos due to appearance concerns, which are appearance-related repetitive behaviors and avoidance.

turns.doctor_question: Have these worries about how you look been making you feel depressed?
turns.patient_response: No, I wouldn't say I feel depressed. I mean, it's... well, it's frustrating, sure. It bothers me when I get stuck at the mirror or when I'm worrying about my hands while I'm trying to work. But it hasn't really brought me down like that, or made me feel sad. I just keep doing my normal routine, it's just more of a nuisance, really.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling depressed, sad, or brought down by their appearance-related worries.

turns.doctor_question: Are you worried that the way your hands or face look means you might have a medical problem or disease?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't think it's a medical problem or a disease or anything like that. I've never really worried that there's something physically wrong with my health causing it. It's just... well, it's just the way they look that bothers me, not that I think I'm sick.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of your concerns about how your hands and face look, do you also find yourself worrying a lot about many other parts of your life?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I mean, I have the usual things, like paying the bills or hoping things go smooth at the plant, but I wouldn't say I worry a lot about them. It's not like... well, it doesn't take up my day. My mind mostly just gets stuck on my hands and my face, like I said. Everything else in my life is pretty normal, I guess. I don't really stress over much else.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient confirms that their mind gets stuck on their hands and face, describing preoccupation with physical appearance.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient denies excessive anxiety or worrying across multiple domains of life, noting they do not stress over much else beyond appearance.

turns.doctor_question: When you check the mirror or adjust your appearance, does it feel like you have to do it to relieve anxiety or to keep something bad from happening?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't think so. I never feel like something bad is going to happen if I don't check the mirror. It's not like I'm scared or anything like that. I just... well, I just look because I want to see how things look, or to see if I can fix my makeup a bit so it doesn't bother me as much. It's really just a habit to check, I guess, not because I'm trying to stop some kind of disaster from happening.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms engaging in repetitive appearance-related behaviors, noting that they check the mirror out of habit to see how they look and fix their makeup so it does not bother them as much.
